courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.actualEvidence: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courses.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courses.contribution: RequiredYear1PPDacademic/researchliteracy,reflection/communityproject; not a specialisedscience/thesis substitute.

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
courses.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling
courses.contribution: Introduces incentives, markets and scarcity for evaluating environmental choices.

courses.name: International Macroeconomics
courses.actualEvidence: Examines short-, medium- and long-run macroeconomic dynamics and policy, including international dimensions. Students study goods, financial and labour markets, inflation and unemployment, economic growth, expectations and the open economy. IS-LM and IS-LM-PC models connect markets and policy effects. Algebraic and graphical analysis and interpretation of macroeconomic indicators support the evaluation of economic developments and fiscal and monetary policy.
courses.methods: Algebraic and graphical macroeconomic analysis; IS-LM and IS-LM-PC modelling; Macroeconomic data and indicator analysis
courses.contribution: Studies aggregate output,growth,inflation,trade andfiscal/monetarypolicy; broad economic context,not a dedicatedenergytransition course.

courses.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courses.actualEvidence: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
courses.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research
courses.contribution: Analyses choice under scarcity and regulation, grounding economic evaluation of resource use.

courses.name: Public Economics
courses.actualEvidence: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
courses.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research
courses.contribution: Studies public goods, externalities, taxation and welfare effects of policy, applicable to environmental decisions.

courses.name: Econometrics
courses.actualEvidence: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courses.contribution: Develops causal and predictive empirical analysis of economic data; environmental application is a possible project, not course-specific.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courses.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courses.contribution: Introduces quantitative research design and statistics for economic or environmental evidence.

courses.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
courses.actualEvidence: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
courses.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions
courses.contribution: Studies algorithm design, data structures, complexity and experimental benchmarking; general computational reasoning complements physical/spatial analysis, not a guaranteed environmental project.

courses.name: Introduction to Data Science
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
courses.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis
courses.contribution: Works with and visualises spatial datasets as evidence for interdisciplinary inquiry.

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
courses.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation
courses.contribution: Applies regression/classification, resampling, regularisation, trees, support-vector and unsupervised methods to real data; general predictive/inferential tools complement GIS/environmental evidence without promising project topics.

courses.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courses.actualEvidence: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
courses.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design
courses.contribution: Builds neural networks in Python/Keras/TensorFlow, including backpropagation, regularisation and image/time-series/text prediction; environmental applications are compositional, not assumed classroom examples.

courses.name: Introduction to Programming
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
courses.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling
courses.contribution: Develops structured and object-oriented Python programming, testing and debugging as the implementation foundation for computational environmental inquiry.

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.actualEvidence: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
courses.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis
courses.contribution: Teaches calculus,integration,complexnumbers anddifferentialequations in appliedprojects; not assumed to cover every VU mathematicaltopic.

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.actualEvidence: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
courses.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica
courses.contribution: Provides probability and statistical inference for quantitative environmental evidence.

courses.name: Building with Nature
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
courses.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls
courses.contribution: Studies nature-based infrastructure across coasts, rivers, cities and ports, using ecological-corridor and intervention-design projects.

courses.name: Living with Water
courses.actualEvidence: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
courses.methods: Site-based water-management case analysis; Comparative appraisal of engineered and nature-based solutions; Context-sensitive adaptation-strategy development
courses.contribution: Studies flood, sea-level and subsidence adaptation through delta water-management projects.

courses.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
courses.actualEvidence: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
courses.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations
courses.contribution: Examines circular-economy recovery technologies, material stewardship and resource security.

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability
courses.actualEvidence: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
courses.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives
courses.contribution: Evaluates how government and non-government stakeholders shape sustainability policy.

courses.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
courses.actualEvidence: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.
courses.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis
courses.contribution: Studies organism diversity, classification and ecological roles using identification, biodiversity indices and a small phylogenetic/data project; it provides biological foundations rather than a full conservation-management course.

courses.name: Dynamic Earth
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.
courses.methods: Geological field observation and measurement; Rock and mineral identification; Geological mapping and profiling; Stratigraphic-column construction; Geological cross-section construction; Sediment and facies interpretation; Geological-history reconstruction
courses.contribution: Studies interacting lithosphere and hydrosphere processes through Earth science and field labs.

courses.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations
courses.actualEvidence: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.
courses.contribution: Analyses natural hazards, exposure, climate-driven risks and adaptation measures.

courses.name: Earth Observation
courses.actualEvidence: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
courses.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design
courses.contribution: Applies ArcGIS Pro georeferencing, projections, queries and surface analysis plus remote-sensing preprocessing/image processing to a collaborative environmental case study.

courses.name: Soils & Aquifers
courses.actualEvidence: Examines soils and shallow aquifers through soil science, environmental chemistry and applied geophysics. Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.
courses.methods: Soil coring and field sampling; Visual soil-structure assessment (grass-VESS); Aggregate-stability, texture and sieve tests; Soil pH, moisture, organic-content and leaching analyses; Microscopy and SEM-EDS; Sample preparation for ICP/IC and interpretation of ICP results; Methylene-blue testing with spectrophotometry/titration; Seismic surveying; Electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveying; Field-data processing in Excel
courses.contribution: Studies soils and aquifers with field and laboratory analysis relevant to water resources and coastal defence.

courses.name: Earth System Science Tools
courses.actualEvidence: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.
courses.contribution: Studies interactingEarthspheres,systemmodelling,proxies andisotopetracers forpast/futureclimate with a greenhouse-gas-pathwaysfieldtrip; description-only evidence considered fully within stated scope.

courses.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
courses.actualEvidence: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.
courses.methods: Geochemical equilibrium and speciation modelling; Geochemist's Workbench; Piper diagrams; Pourbaix and stability diagrams; Laboratory geochemical investigations; Geochemical data interpretation
courses.contribution: Studies aqueous composition, speciation, redox, adsorption and weathering with geochemical modelling and laboratory investigations. Dynamic Earth and Soils & Aquifers precede it; formal prerequisite Sustainability Essentials I is met.

courses.name: Earth's Resources
courses.actualEvidence: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.
courses.contribution: Researches geoscience of geothermal energy, waste storage and carbon capture.

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courses.actualEvidence: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
courses.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement
courses.contribution: Introduces physical and quantitative principles used to examine sustainability systems.

courses.name: Sustainability Essentials II
courses.actualEvidence: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
courses.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design
courses.contribution: Studies waves,chemistry andmaterialscience applied tosustainability, withreflectivejournals/greenwashingproject; foundation foradvancedresourcecourses,not a genericproject substitute.

courses.name: Climate Change
courses.actualEvidence: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
courses.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model
courses.contribution: Examines climate drivers, impacts and adaptation, including sea-level rise.

courses.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
courses.actualEvidence: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
courses.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment
courses.contribution: Compares environmental, social, health and economic consequences across product/process life cycles, including costs and revenues; staged projects culminate in an integrated life-cycle assessment.

courses.name: Energy & Sustainability
courses.actualEvidence: Studies renewable-energy resources, conversion technologies and their integration into sustainable energy systems. Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and biomass resources are evaluated through physical principles, resource availability and generation potential. Storage, electricity grids and demand management connect individual technologies to system reliability. Quantitative exercises, a Polysun workshop, short experiments and local mini-grid work develop the ability to assess energy options in practical environmental and economic contexts.
courses.methods: Renewable-energy resource and yield calculations; Polysun energy-system modelling; Hydropower sizing; Laboratory experimentation on renewable-energy systems; Energy-storage comparison; Mini-grid analysis and design
courses.contribution: Quantifies renewable resources, conversion and storage; applies Polysun modelling, hydropower sizing, experiments and mini-grid analysis to energy options.

courses.name: Renewable System Design
courses.actualEvidence: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
courses.contribution: Designs lower-carbon energy systems with technical and economic assessment.

courses.name: Spatial Planning
courses.actualEvidence: Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.
courses.contribution: Applies spatial engineering, GIS and remote-sensing methods to disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring through hands-on projects; specific techniques beyond the description are not assumed.
